subtitle: Borrowed from medicine — the Apgar score evaluates a newborn's health on 5 dimensions in 60 seconds. The Trade Apgar evaluates a trade setup on 5 dimensions in 60 seconds. Pass score ≥7 with no zeros. This single discipline kills 80% of impulse trades.

blocks.content:
Tier 6 is about EXECUTION — the discipline that turns good analysis into good trades. The biggest gap most traders face isn't knowing what to do; it's actually doing it consistently when emotions, fatigue, and FOMO are pulling in different directions.

The Trade Apgar is a structured pre-trade scorecard. Before clicking Buy/Sell, you score the trade on 5 dimensions, 0-2 points each. Pass: total ≥7 AND no individual zero. Fail: skip the trade. This single discipline filters out the impulse trades that destroy accounts.

rows: Does this setup match my pre-defined criteria? Did I plan it or is it impulse?
2 = pre-planned A-setup. 1 = pre-planned B-setup. 0 = impulse trade not on plan.
Is the risk:reward at least 1:2? Ideally 1:3+?
How many independent signals support this trade? (S/R + candle + volume + indicator + multi-TF alignment + macro etc.)
Is this trade aligned with macro and HTF bias?
2 = fully aligned (macro + HTF + setup all same direction). 1 = neutral. 0 = counter-trend / against macro.
Am I calm, rested, focused? Within my daily loss limit? Not on tilt?
2 = great state. 1 = okay. 0 = tired/emotional/in drawdown/after recent loss.

blocks.title: Scoring rules
blocks.content:
Maximum score: 10 (2 × 5 dimensions).

  • Total ≥ 7 AND no zeros: TRADE
  • Total ≥ 7 but has at least one zero: SKIP (a zero in any dimension is a deal-breaker)
  • Total < 7: SKIP

The 'no zeros' rule is critical. A trade that scores 9 but has a 0 in 'Personal state' (you're on tilt) is a high-quality setup taken at a bad time. Skip it. Wait for both the setup AND the state to align.
Why this works — the discipline mechanism

Impulse trades fail because they're made without explicit reasoning. The trader feels confident, clicks Buy, and rationalizes after. The Apgar inverts this: you MUST score each dimension explicitly BEFORE clicking. This:

  • Forces articulation. If you can't articulate setup quality, you don't have a real setup.
  • Slows down impulse. 60 seconds of scoring is enough to let FOMO/revenge urges fade.
  • Catches state issues. The 'personal state' dimension forces honesty about your current condition.
  • Filters borderline trades. The ≥7 threshold + no-zero rule eliminates the 'maybe' trades that consume risk capital with mediocre EV.

Example 1 — A+ trade that PASSES

  • Setup quality: 2 (pre-planned A-setup from this morning's analysis)
  • R:R: 2 (1:4 — entry $60K, SL $58.5K, TP $66K)
  • Confluences: 2 (4 signals: HTF support + reversal candle + RSI bullish divergence + volume)
  • Macro alignment: 2 (1D uptrend + macro risk-on)
  • Personal state: 2 (rested, calm, fresh from morning routine)
  • Total: 10. No zeros. TRADE.

Example 2 — Setup quality but BAD STATE → SKIP

  • Setup quality: 2 (excellent)
  • R:R: 2 (1:3)
  • Confluences: 1 (some)
  • Macro alignment: 2 (aligned)
  • Personal state: 0 (just had a 2% loss; feeling rushed)
  • Total: 7. BUT has a zero in personal state. SKIP.

The second example: even though the technical setup looked great and the total score reached the threshold, the personal-state zero is a deal-breaker. Trade made on tilt has high failure rate regardless of setup quality.

blocks.title: Don't game the score
blocks.content:
The temptation: you really want to take a trade. You give it generous scores to push the total to ≥7. This defeats the entire purpose.

Honest scoring is the discipline. If you find yourself rationalizing scores upward, that's the signal to step away — not click Buy. The Apgar's value comes from rigorous honesty; gaming it makes it useless.
How to use the Apgar in practice

1. Write the scores down. Don't do it mentally. The journal has an Apgar form on the Futures-AI page — use it. Or keep a paper notebook. Writing forces clarity.
  2. Score BEFORE entering the trade. Not after rationalizing the entry.
  3. Track scores over time. Are your 9-10 trades winning more than your 7-8 trades? If yes, raise your threshold to 8. If no, your scoring may need adjustment.
  4. Review skipped trades. Did the trades you skipped (low Apgar) actually go on to work? If so, examine why you scored them low — maybe your criteria need refinement.
  5. Use it for EVERY trade. 60 seconds × every trade adds up to 0 hours of meaningful overhead but filters out a significant percentage of losing trades.
Customizing the Apgar to your style

The 5-dimension framework is the standard but you can customize for your trading style:

  • Add a 6th dimension if specific to your strategy (e.g., 'time of day' if you trade specific sessions, 'specific indicator condition' if your edge depends on one indicator).
  • Adjust the pass threshold based on your historical data. Some traders need ≥8 to filter their patterns effectively.
  • Adjust the 'no zero' rule to specific dimensions. Maybe a 0 in 'macro alignment' is acceptable for specific counter-trend setups you've validated; but 0 in 'personal state' is never acceptable.

The point is consistency. Whatever your custom scoring becomes, apply it RIGOROUSLY to every trade.

blocks.title: Take this with you
blocks.content:
Three rules:

  1. Score every trade on 5 dimensions BEFORE entering. 60 seconds, written down.
  2. Pass: total ≥ 7 AND no zeros. Otherwise skip.
  3. Don't game the score. Honest rigorous scoring is the discipline. Rationalizing scores upward defeats the purpose.
